text_html: A 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of progressive weakness of her arms and legs. Physical examination shows mild spasticity, weakness, and hyperreflexia of the upper and lower extremities. Motor strength is 3/5 in all extremities. Babinski sign is present bilaterally. MRI of the spine shows a 1.5-cm, well-defined, spherical lesion indenting the spinal cord on the left at the C1 level. This patient most likely has which of the following additional findings?
explanation_html:
Educational Objective: Lesions at the level of the upper cervical spinal cord can affect nearby cranial nerve pathways, particularly the spinal accessory nerve. The spinal accessory nerve innervates the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles, and damage causes ipsilateral weakness in head rotation and shoulder elevation.

Evaluation: Patients with upper motor neuron signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia, and Babinski sign as in this patient’s case) and a focal spinal cord lesion often have additional deficits based on the lesion’s location. A lesion at the C1 level may affect nearby exiting or ascending nerve fibers, including those of the spinal accessory nerve.

Definition: The spinal accessory nerve has a unique course, with spinal roots arising from the upper cervical spinal cord (C1–5) and ascending into the skull before exiting to innervate the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles. A lesion at the C1 level can disrupt these fibers, leading to ipsilateral weakness in head rotation (sternocleidomastoid) and shoulder shrugging (trapezius). The patient’s signs of spasticity, hyperreflexia, and Babinski sign indicate an upper motor neuron lesion due to spinal cord compression. The well-defined mass suggests a slow-growing lesion (eg, meningioma or schwannoma) causing progressive neurologic deficits.

Prevention: There is no specific prevention for spinal cord tumors, but early evaluation of neurologic symptoms can prevent progression of deficits.

Treatment: Treatment may involve surgical resection of the lesion once neurologic deficits develop, often with good outcomes if performed early. Additional therapies may include radiation or glucocorticoids depending on tumor type.

Differential: This patient has a C1 spinal cord lesion with upper motor neuron signs, making involvement of structures originating at that level most likely. Therefore, ipsilateral sternocleidomastoid weakness is the most likely associated finding. The other findings are not directly associated with a C1 spinal cord lesion.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Choice A: Absence of the gag reflex is incorrect. The gag reflex involves the glossopharyngeal nerve and vagus nerve, which originate in the brainstem. A C1 spinal cord lesion would not directly affect these cranial nerves.

Choice B: Loss of taste sensation over the anterior two thirds of the tongue is incorrect. The chorda tympani (a branch of the facial nerve) innervates the anterior two thirds of the tongue regarding sensation. This is unrelated to spinal cord lesions.

Choice C: Paralysis of muscles used for facial expression is incorrect. Most muscles of facial expression are innervated by the trigeminal nerve and facial nerve. A spinal cord lesion would not affect these nerves.

Choice D: Partial hearing loss in the left ear is incorrect. Hearing is controlled mostly by the vestibulocochlear nerve with a contribution from the tensor tympani muscle. This is a cranial nerve not affected by spinal cord lesions.

options.text_html: Loss of taste sensation over the anterior two thirds of the tongue
Paralysis of muscles used for facial expression
Partial hearing loss in the left ear
Weakness of the sternocleidomastoid muscle on the ipsilateral side
